data.title: September FOMC preview: possibility of rate hike, hawkish dot plot, divided Fed
data.description:
With a strong jobs report and a hotter-than-expected core CPI report for August, the Federal Open Market Committee is widely expected to raise its benchmark rate to 3.75%-4.00% from the current target range of 3.50%-3.75% at its September meeting.

"For the Fed, it might have been possible to read the August CPI report as glass half full if nothing else were in the news. The August PPI report released Thursday showed cool increases of healthcare services and portfolio management services, which mostly aren't in the CPI but are in the PCE index that the Fed uses for its two percent target," said Bill Adams, chief U.S. economist at Fifth Third Commercial Bank.

However, the energy price spike overshadows the August inflation reports, according to Adams. "Consumers may experience higher gas prices viscerally as they drive down the street, but core inflation is more vulnerable to diesel price shocks since businesses mainly use diesel to power their truck fleets."

"For the Fed, early September's surging energy prices will probably tip the scale to a hike," said the economist.

Goldman Sachs believes the FOMC will proceed with the hike primarily to avoid the negative market reaction that would likely follow if rates were kept on hold.

However, Michael Strain, director of economic policy studies and senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute, said he does not believe a majority of the FOMC has materially changed its assessment since July, leading him to expect the central bank to leave rates unchanged this week.

Strain acknowledged that the August consumer price index report could have shifted some FOMC members toward favoring a rate increase, but argued that the data would have needed to be significantly more concerning to prompt the Fed to begin a new hiking cycle.

Strain believes most FOMC members could still view the data as consistent with ongoing disinflation rather than a meaningful reacceleration in inflation. The view points to a more divided Fed.

Currently, the probability of a 25-basis-point rate hike at this week's meeting stands at 90.7%, compared with 9.3% odds of maintaining the target rate at 3.50% to 3.75%, according to the CME FedWatch tool.

If effective, the hike will be the Fed's first since July 2023 but unlikely to be the last for this year. A September hike could be the first in a cycle of monetary policy tightening, according to a report by S&P Global Market Intelligence.

This week's meeting is Kevin Warsh's third heading the central bank.

Warsh has staunchly defended his view that the so-called "forward guidance", or signaling the likely direction of the FOMC's policy path, isn't useful.

So, the FOMC statement will likely only provide commentary on the current decision rather than insight into where rates are heading. Therefore, the Summary of Economic Projections, particularly the closely watched "dot plot", will be of significance.

Strategists at TD Securities expect the Fed to raise the policy rate three times in 2026, beginning in September. The previous forecast was that the central bank would hold rates during the year. The SEP projections should be hawkish.

Meanwhile, bond traders price in two hikes this year after the Consumer Price Index report, Bloomberg reported last week.

June dot plot showed the median federal funds rate landing at 3.8% at the end of 2026, compared to the March projection of 3.4%. The September dot plot could see the rate surpass 4.1%.

The question is, can rate hikes bring down inflation that is being driven by energy prices and the AI build-out? Addison Maier, portfolio manager at Janus Henderson Investors, told S&P Global Market Intelligence that hikes cannot impact the price of oil or the outcome of the conflict in Iran, nor change the trajectory of AI spending. However, higher rates could quicken the pace of decline in tariff-driven goods inflation and inflation in the housing sector.

data.title: ResMed upgraded at RBC Capital Markets on Q4 positives
data.description:
RBC Capital Markets on Tuesday upgraded ResMed to Outperform from Sector Perform and raised its price target to $262 from $244, citing positives in the respiratory device maker’s Q4 results for fiscal 2026.

Shares of ResMed fell in early August as investors reacted to its Q4 FY26 report, which, according to RBC analyst Craig Wong-Pan, included a large share buyback program for FY27 and was the first time the company issued revenue and earnings guidance.

Wong-Pan expects the San Diego, California-based MedTech to record high-single-digit earnings per share growth over the next three years despite a potential U.S. return of the rival Philips , which faced a recall of millions of respiratory devices in 2021.

The earnings report, which was also the first for ResMed’s new CFO, Aaron Bloomer, “marked a pivotal change in how the company will be fiscally managed,” wrote the analyst, adding that his upgrade was based on the company’s “positive earnings outlook and an undemanding valuation.”

data.title: Why one Wall Street firm thinks this year's stock-market rally is running out of road
data.description:
By Steve Goldstein

It's one of the first major Wall Street institutions to lower its expectations for stock-market performance since the spring

Wells Fargo strategists lowered their S&P 500 target.

In what may be a first since the early days of the war between the U.S. and Iran, a Wall Street firm is lowering rather than raising its S&P 500 year-end target.

Wells Fargo on Tuesday reduced its S&P 500 target to 7,700 from 7,950, after the index SPX closed Monday just below 7,620, up 11% on the year.

So-called top-down strategist forecasts are not as extensively tracked as Wall Street price targets on individual companies.

Strategists led by Ohsung Kwon said the downgrade comes even as the firm is growing more optimistic on earnings per share - targeting $425 next year for S&P 500 companies and $460 in 2028.

That's very optimistic. In a separate note, Bank of America analysts said the top-down consensus by strategists for 2027 EPS was $392. The so-called bottom-up projection - that is, adding up all the estimates of S&P 500 companies and then weighting by market cap - is $417.

However, the Wells Fargo team said the market is "entering late innings of the cycle, arguing for multiple compression." That refers to the multiple investors assign to each dollar of earnings. While they are not worried about 2027 EPS, they expressed concerns that AI capital expenditure would slow, eating into 2028 earnings.

Wells Fargo says 2027 EPS estimates look extreme.

Wells Fargo argued that 2027 earnings will be "cyclically elevated by 42%" compared with the trendline of what S&P 500 earnings should be at this stage of the economic cycle. The gap of 42% is the highest since the 1950s, they said.

By sector, Wells Fargo is lowering tech to equal-weight from overweight while raising healthcare to overweight from equal-weight. Within tech, Wells Fargo said it prefers software to microchips.

Tech stocks XLK have jumped 28% this year, while healthcare XLV has climbed 9%.

"We see the midterms as a potential risk to tech, especially as political pushback against data centers continues to gain momentum," the firm said.

A potential Democratic sweep would be seen as a positive for healthcare, potentially setting the stage for a restoration of the enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies, the firm added.

Earlier this week, Bank of America increased its year-end target, albeit to levels still below Wells Fargo's new target. BofA sees the index ending at 7,400 - versus 7,100 previously - as it launched a 12-month target of 7,800.

-Steve Goldstein

data.title: US fashion council CEO takes leave after grabbing runway show protesters
data.description:
By Danielle Kaye

The head of the Council of Fashion Designers of America has taken leave from his role after physically restraining animal rights activists at a New York Fashion Week runway show on Sunday, an incident that reverberated online and throughout the city's fashion sector.

Steven Kolb, CEO of the leading U.S. fashion industry trade group, grabbed at least two activists at H&M-owned COS' runway show while they were protesting the brand's use of sheep's wool. He restrained one activist on the ground and covered her mouth with his hand, according to videos viewed by Reuters that circulated widely online.

Kolb apologized for the incident in a statement on Monday. He said he was taking a voluntary leave from work and that he plans to meet with People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals, or PETA, the group behind the protest.

"There is no justification for physically restraining another person. Security should have handled the situation, and I should have stepped back," Kolb said in a statement on his Instagram account.

CFDA, the official organizer of New York Fashion Week, did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the incident and on Kolb's position at the trade group.

PETA is urging H&M and COS to ban wool from their collections, adding in a statement on Sunday that Kolb's actions "show how top people in fashion use violence to silence people" advocating for animal rights.

In a statement, H&M said it only sources animal-derived fibers from certified farms and, where possible, from recycled sources.

"We are deeply sorry about the incident that occurred in connection with our AW26 show on 13 September," a spokesperson for H&M said in a statement. "We respect everyone’s right to express their views, and we believe everyone should be treated with care and respect."

data.title: WSJ Tech Council Summit: CVS Exec Has 'Serious Allergy' to Chief AI Officer Trend — Market Talk
data.description: Tilak Mandadi, chief experience and technology officer at CVS Health, says he has a "serious allergy" to the growing trend of companies appointing chief AI officers. "The problem with associating a person with a technology is that that technology suddenly becomes the solution for everything, because their bonus depends on the adoption of that technology," he says at the WSJ Technology Council Summit. Mandadi says companies should have C-suite roles that prioritize outcomes, instead. That would allow executives to consider a range of tools and strategies, before deciding on which can best achieve the desired effect, he says. (connor.hart@wsj.com)

data.title: India sets 0.4% fee on large merchant payments made via UPI
data.description:
India's payments authority said on Tuesday a 0.4% fee would be levied on transactions worth more than 2,000 rupees (about $20) made to merchants via the homegrown UPI network starting October 15.

The charges will be distributed among the firms facilitating the transactions and are being introduced to bolster investment into infrastructure resilience, innovation, cybersecurity and customer service, the National Payments Corporation of India said in a release.

This comes after India changed its payments legislation on Monday, allowing firms to charge ⁠transactions of more than 2,000 rupees. All payments using the Unified Payments Interface have ​been free so far.

The move is expected to benefit banks and payments firms in Asia's third-largest economy, which posted 24 billion UPI payments totalling $311 billion in August.

The NPCI also said payments made via UPI to specific merchants such as railways, telecom services, insurance and fuel, among others, will attract a flat fee, called merchant discount rate (MDR), of 5 rupees.

For other merchants, the fee on transactions above 75,000 rupees will be capped at 300 rupees.

"Merchants on-boarded cannot pass on MDR charges to customers while accepting payments through UPI," the NPCI said.

The NPCI had met with lenders and payments firms earlier in the day to discuss levying charges on large transactions in the world's ​largest retail fast-payment system, Reuters had reported.

($1 = 95.9550 Indian rupees)

data.title: Gold edges down as oil-driven inflation fears lift rate-hike bets
data.description:
Key points:
  • US central bank's policy decision due on Wednesday
  • Ten-year US Treasury yields hit highest level since 2007
  • Brent crude oil holds above $106 a barrel on Saudi supply concerns

By Noel John

Gold prices fell on Tuesday, pressured by a stronger U.S. dollar and elevated U.S. Treasury yields, as a rally in crude oil prices fuelled inflation worries and bolstered expectations that the Federal Reserve would raise interest rates this week.

Spot gold was down 0.3% at $4,285.88 per ounce, as of 9:23 a.m. EDT (1323 GMT), after hitting its lowest point since August 7 on Monday. U.S. gold futures fell 0.6% to $4,325.80.

"Higher energy prices cause more inflation. More inflation could cause higher interest rates. That's not good for gold ... gold is in kind of a range-bound area. It could actually sell off more if rates continue to move higher," said Daniel Pavilonis, senior market strategist at StoneX.

Traders now await the Fed's rate decision, which is due to be announced at 2 p.m. EDT (1800 GMT) on Wednesday. Financial markets are betting heavily that U.S. central bank policymakers will lift the benchmark overnight interest rate by a quarter of a percentage point to the 3.75%-4.00% range, and signal further tightening ahead. (FEDWATCH)

"I think a lot of (rate-hike fears are) already baked in ... It really depends on what the Fed says afterward. Are they going to continue to raise rates? Are they going to monitor the situation? Overall, it's not a good look for gold," Pavilonis said.

The dollar rose, making greenback-priced bullion more expensive for holders of other currencies, while benchmark 10-year U.S. Treasury yields rose to their highest level since 2007.

While gold is traditionally viewed as a hedge against inflation and geopolitical uncertainty, higher yields on risk-free Treasuries reduce the appeal of the non-yielding metal.

"Much of the hawkish Fed risk appears to be priced in. However, gold could remain vulnerable if policymakers signal rates will stay higher for longer," analysts at ING said in a note.

Oil prices edged higher after attacks on Saudi Arabian energy infrastructure left the kingdom's East-West Pipeline offline, raising fears that damage to energy infrastructure and transport routes could take longer to repair.

Among other metals, spot silver rose 0.7% to $63.64, platinum gained 0.8% to $1,773.13 and palladium was up 0.5% at $1,299.76.

data.title: ICE Canada Morning Comment: Canola Pulling Back
data.description:
WINNIPEG, Manitoba--Intercontinental Exchange canola futures were lower Tuesday morning, due to the mixed nature of the comparable oils.

Crude oil was a pinch higher, providing a little bit of spillover support to the vegetable oils. In Chicago, the soybeans were lower while the oil and meal notched small increases.

European rapeseed was pulling back but Malaysian palm oil was pushing upward.

Statistics Canada is set to issue its first crop production report Wednesday. Although record canola acres were planted this spring, given the varied conditions across the Prairies this growing season it's uncertain if there will be another record harvest or something less than the 21.81 million tonnes gleaned last year.

Last month Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada projected the canola harvest to be 21.6 million tonnes. The U.S. Department of Agriculture estimated the crop at 22.5 million tonnes.

Temperatures across the Prairies Tuesday are to be in the mid-teens Celsius, with rain expected for southern Alberta.

Canola crush margins increased with the November positions between C$272.90 to 283.70 per tonne above the futures.

The Canadian dollar eased back Tuesday morning with the loonie slipping to 71.81 U.S. cents, compared with Monday's close of 71.90.

data.title: Canada to Allow Pension-Fund Investment in Country's Big Airports
data.description:
By Paul Vieira

OTTAWA--Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Tuesday the government is ready to strike deals to hand over operations of the country's four largest airports to institutional investors.

Money raised would be deployed to help build key infrastructure, like new trade corridors, that the country needs, Carney said, as he attempts to reorient its economy and reduce reliance on a protectionist U.S.

In March of last year, Canada said it would open the door to private-sector investment in airports. At present, current rules governing airports have largely prevented private investment in the country's air terminals.

"Canadian pension funds already invest successfully in many airports around the world. It is time to bring that same expertise home to more directly benefit all Canadians," said Carney, unveiling the news at an investment summit he's hosting in Toronto.

Write to Paul Vieira at paul.vieira@wsj.com
